name: English slipware
summary: Red earthenware that English country potters covered with a clear lead glaze and trailed with cream and brown slip. Large dishes, posset pots and jugs carry bold pictures and rhymes.

philosophy.core_thesis: A country potter needs no costly colour: red clay, white slip from a quill, and a lead glaze give a bold picture.
design_principles: Throw the body of a red-firing local clay; the wall is 5 to 8 mm thick.
Cover the front with a white slip when the clay is leather-hard.
Trail liquid slip from a quill pipe in lines 2 to 4 mm wide and in dots.
Draw a picture on a large dish: a king, a mermaid, a pelican or a flower.
Write a name, a date or a rhyme in capital letters round the rim.
Dip the piece in a clear lead glaze; the slip turns cream and the clay turns amber to brown.
Fire the glaze at 1000 to 1080 °C in one firing after the biscuit.
anti_patterns: A white glaze that hides the red clay

form.shape: Large round dishes up to 45 cm wide, posset pots with two handles, tygs (cups with several handles), jugs and bowls.
form.profile: A shallow dish with a wide flat rim and a low well; a jug with a round belly and a pulled strap handle.
form.foot_and_rim: A low foot ring or a flat base; a dish has holes in the rim for a cord; the rim is plain and a little uneven.
form.proportion: Dish diameter 30 to 45 cm; wall 6 to 10 mm; a jug stands 15 to 25 cm high.
rules: Fill the well of a dish with one picture and the rim with a border.
Throw jugs on the wheel; press dishes over a hump mould.
Leave the back of a dish unglazed or lightly glazed.

bodies.rule: Use a local red-firing earthenware with iron in it. A white or vitrified body does not suit this ware: the red clay and the cream slip give the colours.

methods: press moulding over a hump mould
slip trailing from a quill pipe
cutting the foot ring when leather-hard
forming.joins: Pulled handles are luted with slip at the rim and the belly; a posset pot has a spout fixed in a hole cut in the wall.
forming.details: Slip lines in raised relief that the finger can feel, drips of glaze, and a name or a date in rough capitals.

glaze.pattern: Kings and queens, birds, mermaids, tulips and the names of the owners, with a border of dots and lines; some dishes carry a rhyme.
glaze.gloss: A warm gloss of about 50 to 75 GU, with a yellow cast over the cream slip.
glaze.wear: The lead glaze wears at the rim and the foot, and the slip lines stay raised.

palette.strategy: Warm earth colours: cream slip on red clay under a honey-coloured glaze, with a little brown manganese and copper green.

firing.kiln: A coal- or wood-fired bottle kiln; one firing for the biscuit and one for the glaze.
firing.scale: Small family potteries of 3 to 10 workers in Burslem and Wrotham; the large dishes were made to order for feasts and weddings.
firing.signs: Raised slip lines, drips of glaze at the foot, and a signature or a date in capitals on the front.

pieces.form: Wide dish with a trailed picture of a pelican and a dotted border
Bowl with a combed brown and cream pattern
Jug with a round belly, a strap handle and a trailed date
Jar with two handles and an incised and trailed band

positive: name and date in capital letters
rough handmade rim and drips of glaze
still-life museum photograph, soft north light

canonical_works.work: Charger with a king and the name of the potter

emotion.target_response: A warm, rustic cheer: the viewer sees a bold hand-drawn picture on honey-coloured clay and thinks of a farm kitchen.

use_cases: a farm-kitchen set dressing of the 17th century
a museum label on a trailed dish
a rustic bowl or jug brief with a hand-drawn motif
avoid_when: the brief needs a white tin glaze
the brief wants a printed pattern

modifiers.how: Change to a pale pearlware body and turn bands in slip on a lathe; add a mocha tree.
Cover the body with white tin glaze and paint the picture in cobalt.
